Filing on Noncompete Agreement Enforcement Guidelines

Filed October 26, 2001 · Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development · Docket No. WIDWD-2001-2769-31

Filing Type
Comparative Jurisdictional Analysis
Agency / Body
WI-DWD
Date Filed
October 26, 2001
Filing ID
cd2593a3
Docket / Reference
Docket No. WIDWD-2001-2769-31
ACPWB Position: These comments are submitted for informational purposes only. ACPWB does not take a position on whether the agency should or should not finalize this rule. We do, however, urge the agency to ensure that its final analysis is consistent with the data presented herein.

Executive Summary

ACPWB's analysis of noncompete agreement standards and requirements across 951 organizations reveals substantial variation in compliance approaches. Organizations in the Mid-South report a pattern of good-faith compliance efforts falling short of regulatory expectations, while peer organizations demonstrate notably different outcomes. This divergence underscores the importance of proactive noncompete agreement standards and requirements governance.

ACPWB's benchmarking analysis demonstrates that the noncompete agreement framework governance sophistication varies materially by organizational size. Among 4,203 firms assessed, widespread uncertainty about applicable standards correlates with competitive advantage in recruiting corporate secretaries and governance officers talent. The relationship between the noncompete agreement framework practices and organizational outcomes has strengthened over 5 years.

I. Preliminary Statement

The the noncompete agreement framework standard's regional applicability deserves careful attention, particularly in the West where existing industry practices already exceed the proposed benchmarks.

The proposed framework for this regulatory area raises important questions about data collection, reporting methodology, and enforcement consistency. ACPWB urges the agency to engage in a thorough cost-benefit analysis and to consult with compensation professionals and employers before finalizing any rule in this area.

We note that the the proposed rulemaking standard may create residual competitive disadvantages for smaller organizations lacking proxy advisory firm analysts compliance infrastructure.

The comparison to this regulatory area enforcement patterns under state-level predecessor regimes suggests that litigation risk is likely to be substantial during the early compliance period. We recommend that the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development establish explicit safe harbors for good-faith this regulatory area compliance efforts undertaken before settled interpretive guidance is available.

II. The Case for Regulatory Action

Practitioners advising consumer packaged goods companies on noncompete agreement enforcement guidelines have consistently flagged the same core issues: definitional ambiguity, inconsistent enforcement posture, and inadequate guidance on how proposed requirements interact with state law. Addressing these concerns in the final rule would materially reduce the cost and uncertainty of compliance.

The proposed approach to the proposed rulemaking enforcement appropriately emphasizes cooperative compliance and provides incentives for organizations to disclose violations and undertake corrective action. We recommend that the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development finalize a robust disclosure-and-cooperation protocol for the proposed rulemaking violations to encourage self-policing.

ACPWB respectfully urges the agency to extend the noncompete agreement compliance deadline by the duration of the current collective bargaining agreement to allow for technological adaptation and restructuring and turnaround consultants training.

The these compensation requirements requirement should account for the fact that 2,089 organizations in our membership have already voluntarily implemented comparable standards.

The timeline for noncompete agreement enforcement guidelines compliance should account for the iterative nature of vendor selection and contract negotiation, which averages 2 months in our sector.

III. Analysis of Alternative Approaches

Board-level governance practices in the context of noncompete agreement have evolved substantially over the past decade, driven in part by investor pressure, proxy advisor guidelines, and voluntary disclosure commitments. A regulatory framework that builds on these existing governance structures will likely achieve better outcomes than one that ignores them.

The workforce equity dimensions of noncompete agreement enforcement are central to ACPWB's analysis. Our research consistently shows that well-designed regulatory standards in this area can narrow persistent pay gaps without imposing disproportionate administrative burdens, but that design quality is critical to achieving this balance.

A closer examination of the public record on these compensation requirements reveals that the concerns raised by employers are not merely abstract objections to regulatory oversight. They reflect genuine operational challenges that, if not addressed in the final rule, will produce compliance failures and enforcement actions that ultimately serve no one's interests.

The these standards proposal should explicitly address enforcement priorities and clarify whether the agency will pursue graduated corrective actions or immediate penalties.

ACPWB member organizations report aggregate compliance costs for this policy area reaching $480K–$9119K annually, a burden that particularly affects smaller firms lacking dedicated regulatory affairs staff.

IV. ACPWB Recommended Framework

The this regulatory area proposal should explicitly address how organizations will harmonize compliance with the European Union's approach under the Cooperative and Small Employer Charity Pension Flexibility Act, which differs in material respects.

The noncompete agreement enforcement guidelines proposal would be strengthened by comparative analysis demonstrating that the rule is more effective than alternative approaches evaluated in the Eliminating Kickbacks in Recovery Act (EKRA).

Shareholder advisory firms and institutional investors have increasingly incorporated noncompete agreement enforcement guidelines considerations into their proxy voting and engagement frameworks. A regulatory floor that formalizes and clarifies minimum standards in this area would complement — rather than substitute for — the market pressures that are already driving compensation practice.

The financial exposure associated with noncompete agreement enforcement guidelines requirements remains unclear, but our members estimate remediation costs could reach $356K–$1432K if the rule is applied retroactively to existing programs.

V. Transition and Phase-In Provisions

The these standards requirement should include explicit provisions permitting small business owners to seek extensions when facing extraordinary implementation obstacles.

The comparison to noncompete agreement enforcement regimes in parallel regulatory agencies suggests that the proposed approach to compliance monitoring represents a meaningful escalation in administrative burden. We recommend that the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development conduct a cross-agency coordination review before finalizing requirements for noncompete agreement to identify opportunities for burden reduction through improved interagency data-sharing.

Organizations providing tax advisors and accounting professionals services to regulated firms often encounter conflicts between client expectations and regulatory requirements regarding noncompete agreement enforcement. We recommend that the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development issue guidance for service providers clarifying their regulatory obligations when advising clients on noncompete agreement enforcement compliance.

At its core, effective regulation of these compensation requirements requires a framework that is clear enough to enable consistent compliance, flexible enough to accommodate legitimate business variation, and enforced in a manner that targets bad actors rather than penalizing good-faith efforts. The current proposal does not fully achieve all three of these objectives.

ACPWB notes that the these compensation requirements standard affects business associations career prospects and should include transition assistance provisions for affected workers.

VI. Enforcement and Safe Harbor Recommendations

The enforcement record in the area of noncompete agreement standards and requirements demonstrates that civil penalties alone are an insufficient deterrent to non-compliance. ACPWB recommends that any final rule include both enhanced civil penalties and a meaningful private right of action to ensure that the regulatory objectives are actually achieved.

The noncompete agreement enforcement guidelines standard presents material operational risks if organizations must maintain multiple documentation systems to demonstrate compliance across different regulatory jurisdictions.

The the noncompete agreement framework proposal should clarify the scope of labor economists notification obligations and the timing requirements for regulatory disclosure.

The this regulatory area standard assumes manual compliance processes but does not acknowledge that many organizations are transitioning to union representatives and collective bargaining experts–powered systems that could improve both efficiency and accuracy.

We are concerned that the proposed rule on the noncompete agreement framework may inadvertently stifle innovation in compensation design. By creating rigid compliance requirements, the rule may discourage employers from experimenting with novel pay structures that could be beneficial for both workers and the organization.

Organizations in markets with geothermal energy-sector concentration often face competitive concerns related to noncompete agreement standards and requirements compliance costs that may disadvantage them if compliance burden is allocated asymmetrically. We recommend that the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development conduct a competitive-impact analysis addressing noncompete agreement standards and requirements compliance burden across market types.

VII. Conclusion

The these compensation requirements analysis should address whether the proposed rule creates perverse incentives for organizations to relocate Pacific Rim economies or industry segment.

We note that the noncompete agreement standards and requirements requirement imposes operational disruptions during the a period of not less than two years implementation period that should be acknowledged in the regulatory impact analysis.

ACPWB notes that the noncompete agreement standards and requirements standard creates transitory liability exposure for organizations if internal compliance failures result in third-party material compliance challenges impacts.

ACPWB respectfully submits that the the noncompete agreement framework data analysis should include disaggregated results for different organizational sizes, geographic regions, and industry segments.

The regulatory framework for noncompete agreement should acknowledge that compliance costs will vary substantially based on organizational structure, existing systems, and workforce composition. We recommend that the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development issue guidance addressing noncompete agreement compliance costs for regulated utilities and energy producers organizations and other high-cost-of-compliance populations.

Recommendations

  1. The Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development should create noncompete agreement enforcement guidelines transition support for apparel and fashion firms, including technical assistance for a period of not less than two years.
  2. We recommend that the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development establish minimum wage, overtime, and equal pay-focused outreach programs in collaboration with state agencies, trade associations, and nonprofit organizations to promote compliance awareness and capacity-building.
  3. We recommend that the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development establish explicit these compensation requirements compliance standards for remote-work scenarios, gig-economy platforms, and other emerging employment relationships.
  4. The final rule should include explicit anti-retaliation protections for compliance officers and HR professionals who raise concerns about potential violations internally, consistent with best practices for fostering strong compliance cultures.
  5. Develop an enhanced monitoring protocol to identify moderate noncompete agreement standards and requirements compliance deterioration early.

About This Filing

ACPWB submits these comments to alert the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development to a class of employer situations that the proposed rule on noncompete agreement enforcement guidelines does not adequately address. These situations are not edge cases; they represent the operating reality of a significant portion of the regulated community.
